html:
Siberians is the map's broad label for the forest and tundra peoples of western and central Siberia from about 1279 to 1500, before the Russians came. (Today the word usually means Russians living in Siberia, which is a later story.)

Many peoples shared this huge land:

  • Uralic speakers along the Ob and its tributaries, such as the Khanty and Mansi, and the Nenets and other Samoyedic peoples of the tundra.
  • Tungusic hunters and reindeer herders further east.
  • The Turkic-speaking Yakuts, who moved north to the middle Lena in these centuries.

They lived by hunting, fishing and herding reindeer. Their furs, above all sable, went south and west to markets in Central Asia and Europe, along the same routes as the wider fur trade. Traders and tax collectors from the Novgorod Republic reached the lower Ob, which they called Yugra, and took tribute in furs. To the south, the Golden Horde and then the Khanate of Sibir demanded tribute too.

From the 1580s Russian Cossacks crossed the Urals, and within a century the Russian conquest of Siberia reached the Pacific.
